newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Europe peace example to Middle East -- Netanyahu.
newsitem.headline: Europe peace example to Middle East -- Netanyahu.

text.p: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu told a European security summit on Tuesday that it could be an example to the Middle East of how to achieve lasting peace.

Addressing the Lisbon meeting of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), Netanyahu said that, in the 21 years since the body was born in Helsinki, it had played a fundamental role in pacifying a continent until recently split into two hostile camps.
The Israeli leader said that one of the most important principles on which peace in Europe had been founded was the mutual rejection of a resort to violence to resolve differences.

"The first lesson the Middle East can learn from the Helsinki process is that diplomacy must be based on fundamental norms. The most important of these is the absolute commitment of all parties to refrain from the threat or use of force," Netanyahu said.
Earlier, the conference had heard Amr Moussa, the foreign minister of Egypt, which has signed a peace treaty with Israel, reaffirm his country's commitment to ending violence in the region.
But in what was a clear swipe at Israel, Moussa said that lasting peace would only be possible if all countries respected and implemented accords that had been reached.
This was a reference to stalled negotiations between Israel and the Palestinian authorities over the West Bank city of Hebron which Arab leaders say could jeopardise the whole move towards peace.

The Palestinians and their Arab backers accuse the Israelis of dragging their feet over promised troop withdrawals from the city. They also say that the right-wing Tel Aviv government is reneging on a previous Israeli commitment to trade occupied Arab land for peace.

But Netanyahu, who used the opportunity of the summit for a series of meetings with European and North American government leaders, denied at a news conference that Israel was the source of problems plaguing relations with the Palestinians.
He reaffirmed that a deal was "98 percent done" on Hebron and that the only thing holding up a final accord was the reluctance of Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat to sign.
Netanyahu said that the Palestinians had been hoping that, by delaying, it would be possible to generate international pressure on Israel to make greater concessions.

But the Israeli leader, who also denied that his government's commitment to expanding existing West Bank settlements contravened peace accords with the Palestinians, said that he had had a sympathetic hearing from European leaders during his stay in Lisbon.

Netanyahu, who was leaving for Madrid on Tuesday to mark the fifth anniversary of the signing of the Palestinian-Israeli peace deal in the Spanish capital, said that most European countries were clearly bent on being even-handed in their policies towards the Middle East.
"I come away very reassured," he said.
